about: THE WORKS OF 793-1066 - what a merchant house could really pay for, in towns and at home: the 'upgrades' the user asked for. A catalogue of KINDS of work, not of places: a port's own works (places/<port id>.json, 'works') are instances of these kinds with the id '<port id>.work.<id here>', and a chain's grand reward 'unlock_work_<port id>_<id here>' gives one finished. kind: town work (it changes the town and your standing in it; everyone uses it), house work (the house's own), share (a part of something that pays each year). what: two plain sentences. evidence: what was really found or written. where: a list of alternatives: a site kind from BRIEF.md means 'at a site of that kind, in any port'; a port id from ports_793.json means 'anywhere in that port'; 'home' means the house's home port. from/to: the years it can be had. cost_d: deniers, on the money scale of Design/content/CHAINS.md (the debt 480, a small boat about 600, a good voyage 100-300). days: how long the building takes once paid; the house need not wait there. needs and gives: plain words for a programmer to turn into rules. upkeep_d_a_year: due at the winter reckoning; unpaid two winters running, the work is lost. can_be_lost: what can take it, in the words explained under 'lost_words'. got_by: silver (bought when its needs are met), silver or chain (bought, or given finished by a chain), grant (a right silver alone cannot buy: a lord, a reeve, an abbot or a chain gives it, and then the cost is paid). rung: its step on the ladder in Design/works_and_upgrades.md (1 a guest ... 6 a patron). aliases: other plain words a chain may have written after 'unlock_work_<port id>_'. EVERY NUMBER IS A STARTING GUESS TO TUNE. (?) marks what could not be checked against a page. Inscriptions and annals are retold in our own words unless a public-domain translator is named. Written 4 Oct 2026; edit freely.
units: cost_d and upkeep_d_a_year in deniers (d); days in game days; years as in ports_793.json; a 'unit' of goods is the good's own unit in goods_793.json (a cask, a sack, a bolt, a barrel)

lost_words.raid: a 'raid' or 'burning' in chronicle_793.json at that port, or a raiders' card there
lost_words.fire: a town fire: a 'burning' in the chronicle, or a card
lost_words.flood: a river flood: a 'flood' in the chronicle, or the thaw after a hard 'winter'
lost_words.storm flood: the sea over the land: a 'storm' in the chronicle on that coast (26 December 838 in Frisia)
lost_words.ice: a hard 'winter' in the chronicle: the river frozen, the ice breaking up
lost_words.murrain: a 'murrain' in the chronicle (the cattle plague of 810)
lost_words.war: a 'war', 'campaign' or 'battle' in the chronicle at that port or in its realm
lost_words.lord's whim: a new king, count, reeve, abbot or bishop ('accession', 'deposition', 'law' in the chronicle), or the house's standing there falling below 0
lost_words.the river moving: Dorestad only: the Rhine's bed draws away from the bank until the port ends (863)
lost_words.wreck: the ship the share is in is lost
lost_words.a bad partner: a card: the partner cheats, dies in debt or sails off

ladder.name: A guest
ladder.means: you lodge with a host and own nothing in the port

ladder.name: A plot-holder
ladder.means: the reeve knows your strip of ground

ladder.name: A man with a waterfront
ladder.means: she loads at your own door and the house makes things

ladder.name: A man with shares
ladder.means: things pay the house each year without the boat

ladder.name: A householder
ladder.means: the house has a seat, a name and its dead are remembered

ladder.name: A patron
ladder.means: the town and the church are in the house's debt

works.name: A corner of a storehouse, rented
works.what: You pay a householder of the port to keep a few casks and sacks under his roof and behind his door. He answers for them as a host answers for his guest.
works.evidence: A foreign trader lodged with a host who answered for him: the Kentish laws of Hlothhere and Eadric (about 680, c. 15) make the man who houses a trader for three nights answerable for him (?). The scale of a town rent is known from London, where a whole plot paid the king 12 pence a year in 857 (charter S 208). That merchants paid for storage by the year is our inference (?).
works.needs: A port of size 2 or more where the house's standing is not below 0, and a householder willing (act:rent_store).
works.gives: Up to 6 units of goods may be left at this port and taken up again (act:store). They spoil at their usual rate. This is the first way to buy in the cheap season and sell in the dear one.
works.source: Laws of Hlothhere and Eadric 15 (from memory (?)); Electronic Sawyer S 208, https://esawyer.lib.cam.ac.uk/charter/208.html (12 pence a year: verified).

works.name: A plot in the trading place
works.what: A long narrow strip of ground from the street to the water, staked and ditched, with your name known to the reeve. Everything else the house builds in this port stands on it.
works.evidence: Dorestad's excavated harbour was laid out in long plots running to the river, each with its own timber causeway. In London King Burgred sold Bishop Alhhun the plot called Ceolmundingchaga near the west gate in 857, for 60 shillings of silver and 12 pence a year, with the use of scales and weights (S 208). In 889 Alfred and Aethelred gave Bishop Waerferth a court at Hwaetmundes stan, 26 perches long, from the street to the wall (S 346). In 898 or 899 two plots at Aethelred's hithe went with mooring for ships outside the wall, as wide as the plots within it (S 1628).
works.needs: A port of the kind emporium, town or market; standing there of 20 or more, or the reeve's friendship (act:buy_plot). The flag unlock_plot_<port id> gives it free.
works.gives: The house may build house works at this port (storehouse, well, jetty, scales, booth, cellar, sheds). Lodging here costs nothing. Holding a plot counts as the flag unlock_plot_<port id>.
works.source: Electronic Sawyer S 208, S 346, S 1628 (verified); W.A. van Es and W.J.H. Verwers, Excavations at Dorestad 1. The Harbour: Hoogstraat I (1980) (?); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorestad (wooden causeways: verified).

works.name: A storehouse of your own
works.what: A timber house on your plot, floored against the damp, with a door that bars. Goods wait in it for the season when they are dear.
works.evidence: The Dorestad plots carried large timber houses and raised granaries behind the waterfront (?). The trade lived on the gap between seasons: new wine is cheap after the vintage and dear by summer, grain is cheap at harvest and dear in the hungry spring. The capitulary of Nijmegen (806) forbids buying grain at harvest to sell it dear, which shows it was done (?).
works.needs: A plot at this port. Two loads of oak_timber brought by the house take 60 d off the cost.
works.gives: Up to 30 units wait here (act:store). Goods under its roof spoil at half speed. With a factor at this port (unlock_factor_<port id>) they are sold in the dear season at the market price less a tenth.
works.source: Van Es and Verwers 1980 (?); MGH Capit. I no. 46 (Nijmegen 806), as in Design/economy_and_trade.md 1.2 (?); Design/economy_and_trade.md 2.2 (wine about 37 d in November, 91 d in June).

works.name: A sunk cellar for casks
works.what: A pit as long as a boat, lined with planks, under a house on your plot. Casks lie cool in it through the summer.
works.evidence: Plank-lined sunken buildings stand behind the street fronts of English towns from about 900: a row of them at Coppergate in York was built about 975 (?), and others are known in London, Chester and Oxford (?). They are read as stores and workshops under a house.
works.needs: A plot and a storehouse at this port. English and Danish towns first; elsewhere it is likely but not found.
works.gives: Room for 12 casks more. Wine, ale and mead in the cellar do not spoil. What lies in the cellar is kept when the house above burns.
works.source: R.A. Hall and others, Anglo-Scandinavian Occupation at 16-22 Coppergate (York Archaeological Trust, 2014) (?); V. Horsman, C. Milne and G. Milne, Aspects of Saxo-Norman London 1 (1988) (?).

works.name: A jetty of your own
works.what: A causeway of oak piles and planks from your plot out to water deep enough to float her. She loads at your own door.
works.evidence: At Dorestad each plot's timber causeway was built further out, stage by stage, as the river drew away from the bank; the excavation of 1967-77 uncovered a whole waterfront of them (their final length, said to reach some 200 m, is from memory (?)). Hedeby's streets ran down to jetties in the harbour. London's plots at Aethelred's hithe (898 or 899) had mooring as wide as the plot.
works.needs: A plot at the water in this port; the reeve's leave. Three loads of oak_timber brought by the house take 90 d off the cost.
works.gives: No lighterage here: loading and unloading take a day less each call, and no porters need be hired. A ship of deeper draught than the first boat can lie at your plot. Other skippers pay to lie there: about 20 d a year at an emporium, 8 d at a market.
works.source: Van Es and Verwers 1980 (?); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorestad and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedeby (verified); Electronic Sawyer S 1628 (verified); BRIEF_2.md (the example: 600 d, 90 days).

works.name: A well lined with a wine cask
works.what: A shaft dug to the ground water on your plot and lined with an old cask with its ends knocked out. Clean water at the door, for the pot, the brewing and a fire.
works.evidence: Forty-three casks reused as well linings have been studied from Dorestad, of silver fir and oak from the southern Rhineland: the wine came down the river in them. Households there had one or more such wells.
works.needs: A plot at this port, or leave to dig in the market place (then it is a town work and everyone draws from it: act:fund_work). One empty wine cask.
works.gives: Taking on water here costs no time. A fire on your plot takes half of what it would. Dug in the market place for all, it is worth the standing of a small gift (the deed gave_alms, once).
works.source: Archaeology Data Service, Guides to Good Practice: Dendrochronology, case study 'The dendrochronology of the early medieval emporium Dorestad' (wood inventory: 43 barrels, silver fir and oak; verified); D. Eckstein, W.A. van Es and E. Hollstein, 'Beitrag zur Datierung der fruehmittelalterlichen Siedlung Dorestad', BROB 25 (1975) (?).

works.name: Your own scales and weights
works.what: A balance and a set of weights kept at your plot, checked against the port's own and allowed by the reeve. What is weighed at your beam is weighed.
works.evidence: The London plot sold to the bishop of Worcester in 857 went with the scales, weights and measures that were the custom of the port (S 208). The court granted in 889 had its scale and measure free for buying and selling; the tolls taken inside it went to the bishop, those taken in the street to the king (S 346). In the lands of weighed silver every trader carried a folding balance and a set of weights: they lie in graves at Birka and in the harbour at Hedeby (?).
works.needs: A plot at this port, and a grant from the king's reeve or the lord of the market: a chain's reward, or standing 40 there and a gift.
works.gives: No weigh-fee at this port, and no loss on foreign coin or cut silver weighed there (the zone's foreign_loss is nothing for the house here). A deal made at your own beam is a fair one (the deed fair_dealing counts once more each season).
works.source: Electronic Sawyer S 208, S 346, https://esawyer.lib.cam.ac.uk/charter/346.html (verified); trade_rules.json (foreign_loss); the balances at Birka and Hedeby from memory (?).

works.name: A boat shed and a slip
works.what: A long low shed at the head of a slip, open to the water, where she is hauled on rollers for the winter. Sail, oars and rope hang dry under the same roof.
works.evidence: Boat sheds (Old Norse naust) with stone or turf walls and a timber roof, their floors a continuation of the beach, line the shores of Norway; the great ones stand by chieftains' seats such as Avaldsnes on Karmoy (?). In the south ships were hauled out on the bank for the winter; a shed there is likely but not found (?).
works.needs: Ground at the water: a plot, or the home bank. Timber and turf.
works.gives: Hauled under a roof, the boat's wear over winter is halved and a repair here costs a third less. She is ready a week before boats left on the open bank. Spare sailcloth and rope stored here do not rot.
works.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boathouse (naust: verified); O. Grimm, Grossbootshaus: Zentrum und Herrschaft (2006) (?).

works.name: A weaving shed
works.what: A hut sunk knee-deep in the ground, damp enough for the thread, with two upright looms and their clay weights. The women of the house and two hired hands turn wool into cloth over the winter.
works.evidence: Sunken huts with rows of loom weights on the floor are found at trading places and farms all round the North Sea (?). Charlemagne's order for his estates (Capitulare de villis, before 800, c. 43 and 49) has the women's workshops supplied with flax, wool, woad, madder, combs, teasels and soap (?). Frisian cloth (pallia fresonica) was the Frisians' own famous ware, and the new cloth came to market in spring.
works.needs: A plot or a hall; raw wool in the house's store at Martinmas.
works.gives: Each winter up to 4 sacks of raw_wool in the house's store become 2 bolts of frisian_cloth by Lady Day (25 March). With woad or madder in store as well, the cloth sells a fifth dearer.
works.source: MGH Capit. I no. 32 (Capitulare de villis) c. 43, 49 (?); Design/research_trade_seasons_and_hints.md (Frisian cloth new in March and April after the winter's weaving); goods_793.json 'raw_wool', 'frisian_cloth'.

works.name: A quern-dresser's shed
works.what: The black lava querns come down the Rhine as rough blanks. A stone-dresser on your plot cuts the grinding faces and the eye and sells them ready for the hand.
works.evidence: Rough-outs and half-finished querns of Mayen lava have been found at Dorestad and at Hedeby: the stones were shipped unfinished and dressed at the trading place (?). The same lava querns reached London, Ipswich, York and Ribe.
works.needs: A plot at this port; a hired stone-dresser.
works.gives: Quernstones the house sells at this port fetch a fifth more. A commission for querns here can be had in any season.
works.source: S.E. Parkhouse, 'The Dorestad quernstones', BROB 26 (1976) (?); H. Kars, 'Early-medieval Dorestad, an archaeo-petrological study', BROB 30 (1980) (?); goods_793.json 'quernstones'.

works.name: A craftsman's booth on your plot
works.what: A lean-to at the street end of your plot, let to a comb-maker, a bead-maker or a caster of brooches for the season. He pays in pennies and in first pick of what he makes.
works.evidence: The market at Ribe was laid out in the early 700s in narrow plots divided by ditches, and each has the floors and waste of seasonal workshops: comb-makers, bead-makers, bronze-casters, shoemakers (?). Hedeby and Birka show the same (?).
works.needs: A plot at this port.
works.gives: Rent of 18 d a year. Each summer the craftsman offers the house 4 units of his ware (combs, glass_beads or brooches, by the port) a fifth under the market, before he sells to anyone else.
works.source: C. Feveile (ed.), Ribe Studier: Det aeldste Ribe (2006) (?); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ribe (the town ditch of the early 800s: verified; the plots are from memory).

works.name: A higher mound under the house
works.what: The Frisian builds on a mound of sods and dung above the salt marsh and raises it a little every generation. A summer's carting lifts the house, the store and the byre a man's height above the last flood mark.
works.evidence: Some 1,200 dwelling mounds (terpen, wierden) are counted in Friesland and Groningen. A third period of building them began about 700 and went on until sea dykes took over around 1200. On 26 December 838 a storm flood covered almost all Frisia and 2,437 people were counted drowned (Annals of Saint-Bertin 839).
works.needs: A house, a store or a flock of the house's at a port of the Frisian marsh; a dry summer for the carting.
works.gives: A storm flood no longer takes the house's works or stored goods at this place, and a flock share here is driven up and saved. The neighbours who shelter on it remember (standing in the port rises a little after each flood).
works.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terp (1,200 mounds; the third building period from AD 700; dykes about 1200: verified); chronicle_793.json '838-12-26-frisia-flood' (Annales Bertiniani 839).

works.name: A house among your own people abroad
works.what: A small house in a foreign town, in the street where the Frisians live. A man of yours can stay there the year round with a locked chest and a store.
works.evidence: Frisian traders lived in their own quarters up the Rhine: at Worms (829), at Mainz, where the best part of the town, the part where the Frisians lived, burned in 886 (Annals of Fulda), at Duisburg (893) and at Birten by Xanten. A Frisian colony left York about 773 after one of them killed an earl's son (Altfrid, Life of Liudger) (?). A Frisian in London bought a captive in 679 (Bede, Ecclesiastical History IV.22) (?).
works.needs: Standing 20 at that port. For a man to live there: a factor (unlock_factor_<port id>), or a crewman you trust left behind.
works.gives: Room for 20 units of goods. A factor living here buys in the cheap season and sells in the dear one within a purse the house leaves him, and sends a price word home by any ship bound there (as old as her passage). Lodging there is free.
works.source: Annales Fuldenses 886; Frisians at Worms 829, Mainz 886, Duisburg 893, Birten (verified by search; S. Lebecq, Marchands et navigateurs frisons du haut Moyen Age, 1983); Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.11-12 (?); Bede, HE IV.22 (?).

works.name: A hall at home
works.what: A long timber house with a hearth down the middle and benches along the walls, big enough to seat the crew, the kin and a guest of standing. A house with a hall is a house people come to.
works.evidence: The houses on Dorestad's plots and farms were boat-shaped timber halls 20 to 30 m long (?). Archbishop Wulfstan's tract on ranks (1002-1023) counts a seat and an office in the king's hall among the marks of a prospering man worthy of a thegn's rank, and says a merchant who crossed the open sea three times at his own cost was worthy of it too.
works.needs: A plot or the house's own ground at the home port; a building season from Easter to Michaelmas. Ten loads of oak_timber brought by the house take 300 d off the cost.
works.gives: The feast can be held at home (act:feast): the crew's hearts and the house's standing rise. The crew winters with the house and fewer men leave at the reckoning. A partner or a factor can be sworn in here (act:oath). It is needed before a chapel or a gate and bell-house. The heir begins with the standing of a householder, not of a boatman.
works.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ge%C3%BEync%C3%B0o (Wulfstan, 1002-1023: verified; the modern translation quoted there is not used); B. Thorpe, Ancient Laws and Institutes of England (1840), 'Of people's ranks and law'; W.A. van Es and W.J.H. Verwers, Excavations at Dorestad 3 (2009) (?).

works.name: A stone over a grave
works.what: A slab or a small standing stone with a cross and a name, set over one of the house's dead in a churchyard. The priest knows whose it is and so does everyone who walks past.
works.evidence: Small name-stones with a cross and the dead person's name, in runes or Roman letters, were set on graves at Lindisfarne and Hartlepool in the 700s (?). Carved grave slabs of the 900s and 1000s lie under York Minster (?). In Francia a grave near the saints was had by a gift to the church.
works.needs: A dead man of the house or the crew buried in that churchyard (act:bury), and a gift to the church.
works.gives: The dead man can be remembered there (act:remember): the crew's hearts lift, the more if he was one of them. The heir begins with a little standing at that port for each stone of the house there. A man who knows he will have a stone signs on more readily.
works.source: E. Okasha, Hand-list of Anglo-Saxon Non-runic Inscriptions (1971) (?); J. Lang, Corpus of Anglo-Saxon Stone Sculpture 3: York and Eastern Yorkshire (1991) (?).

works.name: A rune stone
works.what: A raised stone, cut by a rune-master and painted, that says who raised it, for whom, and one thing worth saying about him. It stands by a road, a bridge or a thing-place where people pass.
works.evidence: At Mervalla Sigrid raised a stone for her husband Svein, who often sailed a dear cargo ship to Semgallen round Domesnes (Sö 198, 11th century). At Sigtuna the Frisian guild-brothers raised one for Thorkel, their guild-brother (U 379, 11th century). Jarlabanke of Täby raised several for himself while he lived. Most stones are of 980 to 1100; a few are older.
works.needs: A Norse, Danish or Svea port, or one where Northmen have settled; a dead kinsman or partner to name (or yourself, as Jarlabanke did). The line cut on it is the player's own to write.
works.gives: The dead man is remembered wherever Northmen read it: standing with the Norse of that port and its region rises. The heir inherits one friend more from among the dead man's fellows. Men of that port sign on more readily.
works.source: Rundata Sö 198 and U 379 (verified: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltic_area_runestones, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyrkog%C3%A5rden_Runestones, runkartan.se); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jarlabanke_Runestones (verified). Retold in our own words, not quoted.

works.name: The house's names in a book of life
works.what: The monks write the names of the house, living and dead, in the book that lies on their altar, and pray for them by name. In return the house gives, and goes on giving.
works.evidence: Books of brotherhood (liber vitae) were kept from the 700s to the 1200s as registers of those joined to a church's prayers: Salzburg's, Reichenau's, Saint Gall's, Durham's (begun at Lindisfarne about 840 (?)) and the New Minster's at Winchester (1031 (?)). They hold thousands of names of laymen and women.
works.needs: A minster or abbey where the house's standing is 10 or more; a gift in silver, wax, wine or cloth.
works.gives: The house always has lodging and sanctuary there (act:lodge, act:sanctuary). Standing with the church people of that port rises at once, and a little each year the gift is kept up. The heir inherits the entry and the monks' goodwill.
works.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confraternity_book (verified: registers of those in spiritual brotherhood with a church, 8th to 13th century; Saint Gall, Reichenau, Salzburg, Durham, New Minster); the single dates are from memory (?).

works.name: A chapel on your own ground
works.what: A small timber church beside the hall, with an altar the bishop has blessed and a priest the house feeds. It is yours: you built it and your kin are buried at its wall.
works.evidence: Free men built churches on their own land and owned them: the synod of Frankfurt (794, c. 54) lets such churches be given and sold so long as they are not pulled down and Mass is said (?). Herigar, the king's reeve at Birka, 'built a church on his own ancestral property' about 830 (Rimbert, Life of Anskar, 11; Robinson 1921). Earl Odda's chapel at Deerhurst was dedicated on 12 April 1056 for his brother's soul and still stands. Wulfstan's tract names a church among the marks of a man worthy of a thegn's rank.
works.needs: A hall at home; the bishop's leave (standing 30 with the Christians of the home port); a priest to keep. In a heathen king's port it needs his leave as well, and that is a chain's work.
works.gives: Mass at home (act:hear_mass) and a place to bury and remember the house's dead (act:bury, act:remember). The priest reads and writes the house's letters, so a factor's word can come by letter. Standing with Christians at the home port and in its region rises, a little more each year the priest is kept. The heir is baptised, married and known there.
works.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 11, tr. C.H. Robinson (1921), https://sourcebooks.fordham.edu/basis/anskar.asp (quoted; verified); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odda%27s_Chapel (verified); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ge%C3%BEync%C3%B0o (verified); MGH Conc. II.1 (Frankfurt 794) c. 54 (from memory (?)).

works.name: A gate and a bell-house
works.what: A fenced yard round the hall with a timbered gate, and a small tower by the chapel with a bell in it. In English eyes this is what a great man's house has.
works.evidence: Wulfstan's tract on ranks (1002-1023) says a free farmer who throve until he had five hides of his own land, a bell-house and a fortified gate, and a seat and office in the king's hall, was worthy of a thegn's rank; one version adds a church and a kitchen. The same tract says a merchant who crossed the open sea three times at his own cost was worthy of it. Tower churches of the late 900s such as Earls Barton are read as such bell-houses (?).
works.needs: A hall and a chapel at home, in an English port or among the English.
works.gives: A raid on the home port takes half of what it would from the house: the bell warns and the gate holds a while. With the hall and the chapel it makes the house fit for a thegn's rank among the English: the title (a flag unlock_title_thegn) can be asked of the king once the house has also crossed the open sea three times at its own cost.
works.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ge%C3%BEync%C3%B0o (verified); Thorpe 1840; the reading of Earls Barton is from memory (?).

works.name: A causeway to the landing
works.what: A road of logs, brushwood and gravel laid across the wet ground between the landing and the market. Carts and pack-horses reach the ships with dry loads.
works.evidence: The North called such a road a bridge, and building one was a good work. Jarlabanke's at Täby is about 116 m long and 6.4 m wide, with rune stones at both ends saying he made it for his soul. At Ramsund Sigrid made one for the soul of Holmgeir (Sö 101, about 1030). King Harald's bridge at Ravning (the 980s) was 760 m of oak. Dorestad's own waterfront was timber causeways.
works.needs: A port whose landing lies across wet ground; the leave of whoever holds the ground (act:fund_work); timber and brushwood.
works.gives: Loading takes half the time here for every ship, and the market's stock is a tenth larger in the wet months (October to March). Standing in the port rises. Among baptised Northmen after about 1000 it counts as a work for the soul, so the church's goodwill rises too.
works.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jarlabanke_Runestones, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsund_carving (Sö 101), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravning_Bridge (all verified; retold in our own words).

works.name: A fire on the sea-mark
works.what: A watchman, a stack of wood and a hearth of stones on the highest thing by the harbour mouth: a dune, a mound, an old Roman tower. It is lit at dusk when ships are expected, and in fog.
works.evidence: In 811 Charlemagne went to Boulogne to see his fleet, had the old Roman lighthouse there put right and a fire lit on it at night (Royal Frankish Annals 811). The Roman lighthouse at Dover still stood. In Norway King Hakon the Good (about 950) is said to have ordered warning fires on the hills along the coast, but the saga is of about 1230 (?). That a merchant paid for such a fire is our reading, not a record (?).
works.needs: A port on the open coast or behind a bar; the leave of the lord of the shore (act:fund_work).
works.gives: A ship making this port at night or in fog has better odds at the bar by one word (doubtful becomes likely) and loses no day waiting for light. Standing rises with the skippers of every people who use the port. In a year of raids the fire guides raiders too: the port may ask the house to keep it dark.
works.source: Annales regni Francorum 811 (the night fire from memory (?)); https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_d%27Ordre (restored on Charlemagne's order about 810; fell 29 July 1644: verified); Snorri, Hakonar saga goda 20 (?).

works.name: Your stretch of the wall
works.what: A measured length of the town's bank and palisade that the house builds, mends and mans. Every landholder in a walled town owes one, and a rich one can take a long stretch and be thanked for it.
works.evidence: The wall-building order of Worms (about 900) gives the Frisians of the town their own stretch of the wall to keep (?). In Wessex each pole of a borough's wall was manned and mended by four men, one from each hide (the Burghal Hidage, about 914) (?). Bridge-work and fortress-work were owed from all land: Offa's charter of 792 for the Kentish churches keeps them back against the heathen seamen (S 134) (?). Ribe got its town ditch in the early 800s and Hedeby its great bank later.
works.needs: A plot in a port that has a wall or is building one (act:fund_work).
works.gives: What a raid takes from the house's works and stores inside this port is halved, and a small raid takes nothing. Standing rises with the port's lord and its townsfolk. Left unpaid, the stretch is taken back and the standing with it.
works.source: Wormser Mauerbauordnung (from memory: the page would not load (?)); Burghal Hidage (?); Electronic Sawyer S 134 (?); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ribe and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedeby (verified).

works.name: An altar cloth
works.what: A length of fine linen with a silk border, hemmed and given to lie on an altar or to wrap a saint's bones. Everyone at Mass sees it, and the priest says whose gift it was.
works.evidence: The silks in Saint Cuthbert's coffin include gifts King Athelstan made at his shrine in 934 (?). After Byrhtnoth fell at Maldon in 991 his widow gave Ely a hanging worked with his deeds (Liber Eliensis) (?). Silk came north in merchants' packs: English traders bought it at Pavia about 1000 (?).
works.needs: Fine cloth: the price, or a bolt of fine_linen or silk from the hold in its place.
works.gives: Standing with the Christians of the port rises (the deed gave_alms, three times over; a whole bolt of silk, six times). The priest's feeling for the house rises.
works.source: Historia de Sancto Cuthberto 26 (?); Liber Eliensis II.63 (?); Honorantiae civitatis Papiae (?); goods_793.json 'silk', 'fine_linen'; reputation_793.json 'gave_alms'.

works.name: A bell for the church
works.what: A cast bronze bell, hung in a frame by the church door. It is rung for the hours, for the dead, in fog, and when sails are seen that should not be there.
works.evidence: About 854 the Danish king Horik the younger let the church at Sliaswich have a bell, which the heathen had held unlawful before (Rimbert, Life of Anskar, 32). A bronze bell cast about 950 was found in Hedeby's harbour in 1978: the oldest whole church bell known from northern Europe.
works.needs: A church at this port and a bell-founder (in Francia and the Rhineland, or brought from there). Six bars of copper and one of tin brought by the house take 150 d off the cost. In a heathen king's port it needs his leave: at Sliesthorp not before 854, and there it is a chain's work.
works.gives: Standing with the Christians of the port rises much and the priest is the house's friend. Rung in fog, it helps a ship find the landing (as the beacon, in fog only). Rung at a raid, it gives the town an hour: what a raid takes from stores in this port is halved.
works.source: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glocke_von_Haithabu (cast about 950, found 1978; Horik II's leave for a bell, 854: verified); Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 32 (Robinson 1921; the chapter from memory (?)); goods_793.json 'copper', 'tin'.

works.name: A book for a church
works.what: A gospel book or a psalter, written on calfskin by a scribe over most of a year, bound in boards, and laid on an altar with the giver's name in it. It may also be one bought back from men who took it for its cover.
works.evidence: In the later 800s Ealdorman Alfred and his wife Werburg bought the Canterbury gospels now at Stockholm back from a heathen army with their own gold, gave them to Christ Church, and had that written in the book. Bede tells that King Aldfrith gave eight hides of land for one book of the cosmographers (Lives of the Abbots, 15) (?). The goods table reckons a plain book at 360 d.
works.needs: A writing house to make it (a minster or abbey in Northumbria, Francia, the Rhineland or Ireland), or a book already in the hold (goods books: then no cost and no days), or one ransomed from raiders by a card.
works.gives: Standing with the church rises greatly at that port and a little across its region; the bishop or abbot becomes a friend. The house may read there (a text for the chest) and the heir may be schooled there (Latin). A church that has had a book from the house eases its toll for a year.
works.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm_Codex_Aureus (the inscription: verified; retold in our own words); Bede, Historia abbatum 15 (from memory (?)); goods_793.json 'books'.

works.name: A hospice for strangers and the poor
works.what: A house with a hearth, straw and a daily loaf, kept by a church for pilgrims, the sick and those who have nothing. The house that paid for it is prayed for at its door.
works.evidence: Anskar set up a hospital for the poor and the sick at Bremen and gave it the tithes of some villages (Rimbert, Life of Anskar, 35) (?). About 860 Catla of Birka brought her dead mother's wealth to Dorestad, because there were many churches, priests and poor there, and gave it out in alms (the same, 20) (?). The bishops at Meaux in 845 asked the king to restore the hospices founded for Irish pilgrims (?).
works.needs: A church at this port to keep it; standing 20 there (act:fund_work).
works.gives: Standing with the Christians of the port and its region rises much, and the deed gave_alms counts each year it is kept. A sick or hurt man of the crew is healed there for nothing (act:heal). Travellers bring talk: one more rumour at each call. The house's own men lodge free.
works.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 20 and 35 (Robinson 1921; chapter numbers from memory: the full text would not load (?)); Council of Meaux-Paris 845/6 c. 40 (?); reputation_793.json 'gave_alms' (Catla at Dorestad).

works.name: A standing cross in the market
works.what: A tall carved cross of stone or oak where the buying and selling is done. Bargains are struck and oaths sworn at its foot, and the market's peace is under it.
works.evidence: Carved stone crosses were raised by named patrons in Northumbria and Ireland through all these years: Bewcastle and Ruthwell before 800, Muiredach's cross at Monasterboice about 920 (?). In 958 Archbishop Henry of Trier set a cross in his market to show the market right the king had given him; it bears his name and still stands. In German lands such a cross is from then on the sign of a lawful market and its peace.
works.needs: A stone-carver (Northumbria, Ireland, the Rhineland); the leave of the lord of the market (act:fund_work). In the German kingdom after 958 the cross means the lord's own market right, so there it is his to grant.
works.gives: Standing with the townsfolk and the church of the port rises much. A deal struck at the cross is witnessed: a buyer or seller there is less likely by one word to cheat or to break a commission. A fair held under it draws a tenth more stock.
works.source: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marktkreuz_(Trier) (958, Archbishop Heinrich I, market and coinage right from Otto I: verified); R. Cramp (ed.), Corpus of Anglo-Saxon Stone Sculpture (?); the dates of the named crosses are from memory (?).

works.name: A thing-place set out
works.what: A levelled place with a ring of stones and a mound to speak from, where free men meet to hear the law and settle suits. The man who made it is named whenever it is used.
works.evidence: Jarlabanke of Täby had it cut in runes that he made the thing-place and alone owned the whole hundred (U 212, mid 11th century). At Bällsta brothers made a thing-place and raised stones for their father (U 225 and U 226) (?). The assembly itself is far older: the king at Birka put Anskar's mission to it about 852 (Rimbert) (?).
works.needs: A Norse, Danish or Svea port with a thing; standing 30 there; the leave of the chief men (act:fund_work).
works.gives: Standing with the people of that port and its region rises much. When the house has a suit there (act:lawsuit) its odds are one word better, and the law is spoken to the house without a gift (act:hear_law).
works.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jarlabanke_Runestones (U 212 side B: verified); Rundata U 225, U 226 (?); Rimbert, Vita Anskarii 26-27 (?).

works.name: A burned church made new
works.what: After the raiders have gone the church stands roofless and no one has the silver to raise it. You buy what is left and have it built again from the ground.
works.evidence: The sundial over the door at Kirkdale says that Orm, Gamal's son, bought Saint Gregory's minster when it was all broken and fallen and had it made new from the ground, in the days of King Edward and Earl Tostig (1055-1065). Free men owned the churches they built (Frankfurt 794, c. 54) (?). The raids left many to rebuild: Lindisfarne in 793, Dorestad four years running from 834, Hamburg in 845.
works.needs: A port whose church has been burned in a raid or a fire (the chronicle), and the bishop's leave (act:fund_work).
works.gives: The church is the house's own: the house names its priest and is buried there. Standing with the Christians of the port and its region rises greatly, and the bishop is a friend to the heir too. The port's church site works again, with its feast days.
works.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirkdale_sundial (verified; retold in our own words); MGH Conc. II.1 (Frankfurt 794) c. 54 (?); chronicle_793.json (the raids).

works.name: A share in another man's ship
works.what: You put silver into another skipper's venture and take that part of what she makes. If she is lost, so is the share.
works.evidence: Northmen who pooled their goods for a voyage were felagar, fellows, and the word is cut on rune stones raised by partners for partners (?). The Frisian guild-brothers of Sigtuna raised a stone for one of their own (U 379). Sigrid's husband Svein had his own cargo ship on the run to Semgallen (Sö 198). In the Frankish lands the evidence for such partnerships is thin (?).
works.needs: A skipper who knows the house: his feeling friendly, or a partner won in a chain (unlock_partner_<name>). An oath before witnesses (act:oath).
works.gives: Each Martinmas a quarter of what her year made: most years 40 to 80 d, in a bad year a loss of up to 40 d, in a great year up to 150 d. Her skipper gives the house his price words when they meet. If she is wrecked or taken the share is gone.
works.source: Rundata U 379, Sö 198 (verified); J. Jesch, Ships and Men in the Late Viking Age (2001), on felag (?); Design/economy_and_trade.md 4 ('thin evidence in the north').

works.name: Sheep on the salt marsh
works.what: Forty ewes on the grazing outside the mound, kept by a shepherd for half the wool and half the lambs. The other half is yours at shearing.
works.evidence: The Frisian marsh was sheep and cattle country, and its wool became the cloth the Frisians were known for: the Frisian lands of the abbeys of Fulda and Werden paid their dues in bolts of cloth (?). The cattle plague of 810 ran through the whole empire (Royal Frankish Annals 810), and the flood of 838 drowned beasts with the people. English law reckons a sheep at 5 pence (VI Athelstan) (?).
works.needs: Marsh or down grazing and a shepherd on halves; in Frisia a mound to drive them to.
works.gives: Each June at shearing 3 sacks of raw_wool and 4 wheels of cheese wait for the house. With a weaving shed the wool goes straight to the looms. Unfetched, it is sold there at the cheap price.
works.source: Annales regni Francorum 810; chronicle_793.json '838-12-26-frisia-flood'; Traditiones Fuldenses (the Frisian dues in cloth) (?); VI Athelstan 6.2, as in Design/economy_and_trade.md (?).

works.name: A fish weir
works.what: Two long fences of stakes and wattle set in a V across the tide or the stream, with a basket at the point. The ebb leaves the fish in it.
works.evidence: The survey of Tidenham on the Severn (between 956 and 1065) counts the estate's weirs hamlet by hamlet: thirty basket weirs at Stroat, fourteen at Milton with two hackle weirs on the Wye, twenty-one at Kingston with twelve on the Wye. It adds that every other fish, and every rare fish, belongs to the lord (?). Timber weirs of the 600s to 900s still stand in the mud of the Blackwater in Essex (?).
works.needs: A tidal shore or a river with an eel run; the leave of the lord of the water, who takes every other fish.
works.gives: Each autumn, in the eel run from Michaelmas to Martinmas, 6 barrels of eels wait at the weir (the house's half, salted). On a salmon river, a barrel of salmon in spring as well. Unfetched fish is sold there at the cheap price.
works.source: Electronic Sawyer S 1555, https://esawyer.lib.cam.ac.uk/charter/1555.html (bounds and customs of Tidenham; the weir counts verified by search; the lord's half from memory (?)); Historic England, River Fisheries and Coastal Fish Weirs (2018); the Blackwater dates from memory (?).

works.name: A share in a water mill
works.what: A quarter of a mill on a stream: the wheel, the stones, the pond and the miller's toll of every sack ground. The lord or the abbey holds the rest.
works.evidence: Domesday Book (1086) counts 5,624 water mills in England, many held in halves, thirds and quarters, each with a yearly value: the mill at South Ferriby on the Humber was worth 10 shillings. The estate book of Saint-Germain-des-Prés (about 825) lists dozens of mills and their rents in grain (?). A mill of the 800s with a horizontal wheel was dug at Tamworth (?).
works.needs: A lord, an abbey or a kin group willing to sell a share: standing 20 at the port. A river with fall, or a tide.
works.gives: Each Michaelmas a quarter of the toll: 4 sacks of flour at the mill, or 30 d if the house does not fetch them. The house's own grain is ground there free (wheat or rye into flour, for ship's bread).
works.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watermill (Domesday: 5,624 mills: verified); https://opendomesday.org/place/SE9820/south-ferriby/ (1 mill, value 10 shillings: verified); Polyptych of Irminon (?); P. Rahtz and R. Meeson, An Anglo-Saxon Watermill at Tamworth (1992) (?). The fractions of mills in Domesday are from memory (?).

works.name: A salt pan
works.what: On the Frisian and Zeeland shore salt is got by burning sea-soaked peat and boiling the ash in sea water, and on the bay of the Loire the sun dries it in clay beds. A pan with its hut and its boilers is a thing that is bought, sold and given.
works.evidence: In 776 a man called Godebert gave the abbey of Lorsch seventeen 'kitchens for making salt' (culinae ad sal faciendum) in Zeeland, probably on Schouwen. The abbey of Redon's charters of the 850s and 860s record laymen selling and giving salt pans at Guérande (?). At Droitwich the brine-houses belonged in shares to manors far away (Domesday Book) (?).
works.needs: A salt shore (Zeeland, Frisia, the Loire bay) or a brine spring; the leave of the lord of the shore; fuel.
works.gives: Each autumn 16 sacks of salt wait at the pan (sea_salt on a shore, brine_salt at a spring). Unfetched salt is sold there at the cheap price. Salt is dear inland and before the autumn slaughter.
works.source: Codex Laureshamensis, the gift of 776 (verified by search: Godebert, 17 culinae, Zeeland; natuurtijdschriften.nl, Grondboor en Hamer 2009); Cartulaire de Redon (?); Domesday Book, Worcestershire (?); goods_793.json 'sea_salt', 'brine_salt'.

works.name: A share in a vineyard up the Rhine
works.what: A strip of vines on a south slope above the river, worked by a vine-dresser for half the crop. Your half lies in the press-house in casks of fir when you come for it.
works.evidence: The abbeys of Lorsch and Prüm held vineyards by the hundred along the Rhine and the Mosel, given strip by strip by laymen (the Lorsch codex; Prüm's survey of 893) (?). Frisian traders lived at Worms and Mainz, in the wine country, and the casks that ended as well linings at Dorestad were of silver fir from the upper Rhine. Round Paris the estate book of Saint-Germain-des-Prés counts vineyards on nearly every estate (?).
works.needs: A house or a host among your own people in that town (the work factor_house, or standing 30 there); a seller, most often an abbey leasing for a life.
works.gives: Each year at Martinmas 3 casks of new wine wait in the press-house (rhenish_wine at Mogontia, frankish_wine at Parisius): none in a frost year, 5 in a great one. New wine is cheap where it is made and dear down river by summer.
works.source: ADS dendrochronology case study, Dorestad (silver fir casks: verified); Annales Fuldenses 886 and the Frisians at Worms 829 (verified by search; Lebecq 1983); Pruemer Urbar 893 (?); Codex Laureshamensis (?); Polyptych of Irminon (?).

works.name: A ferry right
works.what: The right to keep the boat at a river crossing and take the fare from every man, horse and cart. It belongs to the lord of the bank, and he gives it or sells it.
works.evidence: A crossing was a lord's income like a mill or a toll. Charlemagne's capitulary of 805 forbids new tolls at bridges and ferries where none were taken of old (?). The toll list of Raffelstetten (about 904) sets what is paid on the Danube (?). Domesday Book values ferries on the Humber and the Trent by the year (?). In 777 Charlemagne gave the church of Utrecht the bank dues at Dorestad (?).
works.needs: The grant of the lord of the bank: a chain's reward, or standing 40 in that realm and a gift. A ferry barge (ship class ferry_barge) and a ferryman.
works.gives: About 80 d a year in fares, paid at the winter reckoning. The house crosses free (act:cross). The ferryman hears everyone: one more rumour at each call there. A bridge built at the crossing ends it.
works.source: MGH Capit. I no. 44 (Thionville 805) c. 13 (?); Inquisitio de theloneis Raffelstettensis (?); Domesday Book, Lincolnshire (the South Ferriby entry shows no ferry: checked; the others are from memory (?)); MGH DD Kar. 1 no. 117 (777) (?); ship_classes_793.json 'ferry_barge'.

works.name: A pier of the bridge
works.what: A timber bridge is kept up pier by pier, each pier the charge of named men. The house takes one pier and its span: the piles, the beams and the planks.
works.evidence: The bridge-work list of Rochester (copied about 1120 from an older English text) names the estates that owe each of the nine piers and how many beams and planks each must lay (?). Bridge-work was owed from all land in England. London's bridge is there again by about 1000, when ships paid toll at it (IV Aethelred) (?). Charlemagne's timber bridge over the Rhine at Mainz took ten years to build and burned in three hours in May 813 (Einhard, 17 and 32).
works.needs: A port with a bridge, or one building a bridge; the reeve's leave (act:fund_work).
works.gives: The bridge toll, and the toll for passing under it, are forgiven the house there for good. Standing rises with the port's lord and its townsfolk. Among baptised Northmen it is a work for the soul.
works.source: Textus Roffensis, the Rochester bridge-work list (?); IV Aethelred 2 (?); Einhard, Vita Karoli 17, 32 (tr. S.E. Turner, 1880); Annales regni Francorum 813.

works.name: A booth at the fair
works.what: A set place in the rows at a fair, with your own posts and awning, held from year to year from the lord of the fair. You sell from the first morning, not from the back of a cart on the third.
works.evidence: The fair of Saint-Denis opened on the saint's day, 9 October, and ran for weeks. King Pippin's judgment of 753 gives its tolls to the abbey and names Saxons and Frisians among those who came to buy wine and honey (?). The market plots of Ribe and Kaupang were used in the summer season only.
works.needs: The grant of the fair's lord (at Saint-Denis the abbot): a chain's reward, or standing 20 there and the yearly due.
works.gives: At that fair the first 10 units the house sells do not push the price down, and there is no stall fee. The abbey's or the king's peace covers the house on the way to the fair and back.
works.source: MGH DD Kar. 1 no. 6 (Pippin, 753) (?); fairs_793.json (the five fairs and their days).

works.name: A seat among the sworn merchants
works.what: The merchants of the town swear to stand by each other, keep a common chest, and drink together on set days. A seat costs an entry gift and your share of every feast.
works.evidence: About 1020 the monk Alpert of Metz wrote sourly of the merchants of Tiel that they judged by their own custom, swore each other clear, and put their money together for feasts (?). The Frisian guild-brothers of Sigtuna raised a rune stone for a dead brother (U 379, 11th century). In England the thegn Orc gave his guild at Abbotsbury its hall, and its rules survive (about 1040).
works.needs: The year 1000 or later. A plot in the port, standing 30 there, and two brothers to speak for the house: or a title won in a chain (unlock_title_<name>).
works.gives: In a suit in that port the brothers swear with the house: its odds are one word better (act:lawsuit, act:oath). After a wreck the common chest lends the house up to 300 d with no day set. A dead brother is buried and remembered at the guild's cost.
works.source: Alpert of Metz, De diversitate temporum II.20 (?); Rundata U 379 (verified); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbotsbury_Abbey (Orc's guild and its hall: verified); BRIEF.md rule 2 (no guilds by that name before about 1000).
